785.title: Brigid of Kildare
785.hook: an Irish abbess famed for giving away everything, even her father's sword
785.howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox Christians honor Brigid as a saint, and in Ireland people weave Brigid's crosses from rushes around her feast day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patrick, the captive who went back. Your line was the voice of the irish.

Food from the house, butter from the kitchen: a girl keeps giving her father's things away to anyone poor who asks, and he's had enough. He drives her to a king's hall to sell her, and goes inside, leaving his sword in the chariot. While he's in there, a poor man comes by and asks for help. The girl has nothing of her own. So she hands him her father's sword. Her name is Brigid.

That's the story as the old Lives of Brigid tell it, and it's worth being plain about what those are. They aren't diaries. They're Lives written by monks, Cogitosus among them, after her time, gathering what Ireland remembered and loved about her. Read that way, they're a portrait, and nearly every brushstroke is the same color: she gives. When her father finds the sword gone, he's furious, and the king asks the girl why she gives away her father's goods. Brigid answers, in the story, that if she had the king's whole treasure, she would give it all to Christ, through the poor. And the king lets her go. A girl like that, he decides, is not one to keep. She becomes a nun, and an abbess. The Lives tell of her church at Kildare, a community of women and men, of guests fed, butter that didn't run out, and a table kept open. Irish tradition gives her a striking title: Mary of the Gael. Mary, the mother of Jesus, for the Irish: a mother to them, close and generous. Behind the stories stand lines from the Gospels. Jesus says, in the King James: "Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away." And in Acts, Paul recalls a saying of Jesus: "It is more blessed to give than to receive." Brigid's stories take those lines as far as they will go. Not the spare coat. The father's sword. Some readers smile at the miracles in the Lives; others treasure them. Either way the picture holds: a woman whose hands kept opening.

Look, in your mind, around the place you live, past the junk drawer, for something you actually use: a good coat, a tool, a book you love, a free afternoon. Picture who could use it, a neighbor, a shelter, a friend starting over, and notice what happens in you as you imagine handing it over. If you pray, offer it to God before you offer it to them.
Brigid. The Irish abbess remembered, story after story, for giving things away, even her father's sword.
Your line: mary of the gael. A mother to the Irish, with open hands. Rest well.

786.title: Benedict
786.hook: a young man flees Rome's chaos for a cave, then writes a rule of life for monks
786.carry: listen, with the ear of the heart
786.howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns, in Catholic, Anglican and other communities, live by the Rule of Benedict and read from it together, and some lay Christians follow its pattern of prayer, work and hospitality as oblates.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brigid, who gave away even her father's sword. Your line was mary of the gael.

Bread comes down on a rope, with a little bell tied on so the man below will know it's coming. He's living alone in a cave in the hills, and a monk nearby keeps him fed. Not long before, he was a student in Rome, from a good family. He looked at the city, and at the students around him, and was afraid that if he stayed, he'd go over the same edge they were going over. So he walked away from his books and his prospects. The young man is Benedict.
screen: `BREAD ON A ROPE, AND A BELL.`

segments.voice: His early life comes from Gregory the Great, a pope who wrote it down in a book of stories called the Dialogues. Gregory's Benedict is full of wonders. But what Benedict himself left behind is quieter: a Rule, a short book about how monks should live together. Here's how it begins, in its Latin: Ausculta, o fili. Listen, my son, to the master's teaching, and incline the ear of your heart. Listen is the first word. Not obey. Not work. Listen, and with the ear of the heart. The Rule keeps turning to scripture. Early on it takes up a psalm, in the King James words: "To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your heart." Then it gets practical. When to pray, through the day and the night. When to eat, how much, and when to keep silent. How to choose an abbot, and why the abbot should call everyone to counsel, even the youngest, because, the Rule says, the Lord often shows what is better to the younger. How to welcome guests: each one received as Christ, because Christ will say, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." The Rule hopes to set down nothing harsh, nothing burdensome. It calls itself a little rule for beginners. One thing often said about Benedict isn't his: the motto ora et labora, pray and work. It's a fair summary of the life, but those words aren't in the Rule. What's in the Rule is the first word, and communities that follow it, Catholic, Anglican and others, still read from it together.

Start where Benedict starts: listen, and ask what the ear of your heart is hearing about how your days are going. Maybe it's more sleep, one meal without a screen, a few quiet minutes in the morning; let one simple line come, short and gentle, nothing harsh, nothing burdensome. If you pray, offer that line to God.
Benedict. The young man who left Rome for a cave, and wrote a rule of life that begins with one word: listen.
Your line: listen, with the ear of the heart. One word, and a whole way of life after it. Day seven hundred eighty-six, done.

787.title: Scholastica's storm
787.hook: Benedict's sister prays for rain so he'll stay and talk, and a storm keeps him
787.howItsDone: Christians who keep the old calendar of saints remember Saint Scholastica as Benedict's sister, and Benedictine communities keep her feast and retell the story of the storm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict, and a Rule that begins with listen. Your line was listen, with the ear of the heart.
screen: `LISTEN, WITH THE EAR OF THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Supper is finished. The candles are low. A brother and a sister sit across a table in a small house near his monastery, and they have talked all day about God. In the story, this is their custom: she comes to see him once a year, and they spend the whole day in praise and holy conversation. Now it's dark. She asks him to stay the night and keep talking until morning. He says no. He's the man who wrote the rule, and he says he cannot spend the night outside his monastery. So the sister folds her hands on the table, rests her head on them, and prays. The sky outside is clear.
screen: `ONE DAY A YEAR, TALKING ABOUT GOD.`

segments.voice: The sister is Scholastica, and the story comes from Pope Gregory the Great, who wrote down the life of her brother Benedict. When Scholastica lifts her head, Gregory says, the thunder breaks, the lightning flashes, and the rain comes down so hard that Benedict and the brothers with him can't put a foot out the door. Benedict is upset. In Gregory's telling he says, more or less, God forgive you, sister, what have you done? And she answers: I asked you, and you wouldn't listen. So I asked my God, and he listened. Now go, if you can. He can't. So they stay up all night, and the story says they filled each other with holy conversation until dawn. Why did her prayer win? He was the holier man, wasn't he? Gregory doesn't answer that way. He quotes the letter of John: "God is love." Then comes the line that gives today's carry: she could do more, because she loved more. Notice what the story doesn't do. It doesn't say Benedict's rule was wrong. It says that on one night, love outweighed it. Gregory adds a quiet ending. Three days later, Benedict, standing in his cell, sees his sister's soul rise toward heaven like a dove. He has her buried in the tomb he had made ready for himself. That was the last time they talked.
screen: `I ASKED MY GOD, AND HE LISTENED.`
`SHE COULD DO MORE: SHE LOVED MORE.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you usually leave a little early: the call you end first, the visit you cut short because there's a schedule, a rule, a reason. Picture them across the table, and without fixing anything, notice what you might hear if you stayed ten more minutes. If you pray, name them before God.
Scholastica's storm. The night a sister's prayer kept her brother at the table, because, as Gregory tells it, she loved more.
Your line: she loved more. A clear sky, a sudden storm, and a whole night of talk. See you tomorrow.

788.title: Columba on Iona
788.hook: an Irish monk exiled to an island founds a mission that reaches Scotland
788.howItsDone: Christians in Scotland and Ireland remember Saint Columba, also called Colum Cille, and Iona still draws pilgrims and an ecumenical community that keeps a daily rhythm of prayer there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sister's prayer and a sudden storm. Your line was she loved more.

A gray bird drops out of the sky onto a beach. It's a crane, worn out from a long flight over the sea, too tired to move. Somebody saw this coming. A few days before, the abbot of the island told one of his monks: go down to the western shore and watch. A crane will come from Ireland, blown off course and exhausted. Carry it to a house nearby, feed it, look after it for three days. Then it will fly home. And it does. The abbot who sent him had come from Ireland too, and made this island his home. His name was Columba.

The crane story comes from Adomnán, a later abbot of the same island, who wrote a life of Columba. In Adomnán's telling, Columba blesses the bird because it came from the land of their fathers. Why did Columba leave? Adomnán says simply that he sailed from Ireland wishing to be a pilgrim for Christ. Later tradition tells a sharper story, of a quarrel and a battle, and an exile laid on him as penance. The old sources don't settle it. Here is what is known. He came to a small island off the west coast of what is now Scotland, called Iona, and with his companions built a monastery there. Bede, the English monk and historian, writes that Columba came to preach the word of God to the northern Picts, and that the island was given to him for a monastery. From that small place, monks went out. Bede tells how one of them, Aidan, went from Iona to the English king Oswald in Northumbria, and set up a monastery on another island, Lindisfarne. So a monk who left home became the start of a long chain of homes for others. Adomnán's Latin for what Columba wanted is peregrinatio, pilgrimage. Some readers hear in it more than a trip with a return ticket: leaving home for Christ and not coming back, an exile chosen and offered. In Columba's last days, Adomnán says, a white horse came and laid its head against him and wept. The horse, he says, knew its master was leaving.

Find a quiet place: a parked car, a back step, or just close your eyes where you are. Let the noise of the day be the sea around the island, still there but out past the shore, and notice one thing that came to you from far away today, the way the crane came: a message, a memory, a worry. Look after it for a minute, and if you pray, hand it to God.
Columba. The Irish monk who left home as a pilgrim for Christ, and built a monastery on Iona that sent others out.
Your line: the island mission. One small island, and monks going out from it. That's day seven hundred eighty-eight.

789.title: Gregory the Great
789.hook: a pope who called himself servant of the servants of God
789.howItsDone: Catholics honor Gregory the Great as a pope and Doctor of the Church, and Orthodox Christians honor him as Saint Gregory the Dialogist; the plainchant called Gregorian chant is named after him by tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Columba, the pilgrim for Christ, and his island. Your line was the island mission.

Old letters open with a name and a title. Dear Sir. From the Office of the Director. Titles tell you where someone stands. The man who wrote down Scholastica's storm was a bishop of Rome, a pope, and he signed his letters with a title of his own choosing. Not lord of the church. Not head of anything. He called himself servant of the servants of God. It was harder to live than to write.

His name was Gregory, and later Christians called him the Great. Before he was pope, he had been a monk. He turned his family's house in Rome into a monastery, and he loved the quiet there. Then he was made bishop of Rome, and the quiet ended. Bede passes on Gregory's own complaint: the cares of his office pulled his mind away from prayer, like a ship tossed in a storm, looking back at the shore it had left. So he knew what the job could do to a person. He wrote a whole book about it, the Pastoral Rule, a guide for anyone who leads souls. One of its warnings is that the person at the top is in special danger of pride. And the title: Servus servorum Dei, servant of the servants of God. It echoes what Jesus told his friends when two of them asked for the places of honor beside him. In Mark's Gospel he says, "whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all." Gregory put that at the top of his letters, where everyone would see it, including him. Christians remember him in different ways. Catholics count him among the great popes and teachers of the church. Orthodox Christians honor him too, as Saint Gregory the Dialogist, after the book where Benedict's story is told. And a thread for tomorrow: Gregory is the one who sent monks to England. A title is a promise made in public. His said: I'm here to serve those who serve God.

Think of the people who make your day work and rarely get thanked: whoever cleans the building, drives the bus, answers the phones, stocks the shelves. Pick one, imagine what their day is like, and find one small way to serve them back: learning their name, a proper thank-you, a job made easier by a minute. If you pray, pray for them by name.
Gregory. The monk who became pope, later called the Great, and signed himself servant of the servants of God.
Your line: servant of servants. A title he put where he would see it too. Until tomorrow.

790.title: Augustine of Canterbury
790.hook: sent from Rome to England, he's told: don't destroy their temples, bless them
790.howItsDone: Anglican and Catholic Christians remember Augustine of Canterbury as the monk sent by Gregory to Kent, and the archbishop of Canterbury's chair is traditionally called the chair of Saint Augustine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory, servant of the servants of God. Your line was servant of servants.

On the road, they lose their nerve. A group of monks has left Rome on Gregory's orders, headed for the far island of the English. Bede, who tells the story, says fear seized them: a fierce, unbelieving people, a language none of them could speak. So they stop, and send their leader back to ask the pope to call the whole thing off. Their leader is a monk named Augustine. Not the Augustine of the Confessions; another Augustine. Gregory sends him back with a letter that says, more or less, keep going: better not to start a good work than to turn back from it. So they go on.
screen: `ON THE ROAD, THEY LOSE THEIR NERVE.`
`ASK THE POPE TO CALL IT OFF.`

segments.voice: They land in Kent, and the king, Ethelbert, comes to meet them. Bede says he insisted on the open air, in case they tried some kind of magic indoors. The monks walk up carrying a silver cross and a picture of Christ painted on a board, singing as they come. The king's answer is careful and fair. Your words are good, he says, but they're new to me, and I can't just leave what my people have always held. But you've come a long way. Stay. We'll feed you, and you can speak to anyone who will listen. Later, Gregory writes a letter about what to do with the old temples of the English. Bede keeps it. Gregory says he has thought about it for a long time. Don't tear the temples down. Take out the idols, bless the buildings with water, set up altars, and let them become places of worship to God, so people can keep coming to the places they already know. Even their old feast days should become feasts of thanksgiving. Then a sentence about how people change: whoever wants to climb a high place goes up step by step, not in leaps. Two cautions. Bede also keeps an earlier letter in which Gregory urged the king to overthrow the shrines, so this was a change of mind, not his only word. And it was still a mission: the old gods' images were removed. But in the later letter Gregory chose to keep what he could: the buildings, the gathering places, the habit of feasting together.

Picture a place you've been trying to change: a team at work, a family habit, a neighborhood. Before you think about what's wrong with it, find one thing that's already good there, a gathering, a tradition, a person who keeps it going, and see it clearly. If you pray, give thanks for it; if not, just name it to yourself.
Augustine. The monk who nearly turned back, reached Kent, and carried Gregory's advice: keep the old places, and bless them.
Your line: bless, don't destroy. Not in leaps, but step by step. Day seven hundred ninety, done.

791.title: Hilda of Whitby
791.hook: a wise abbess who led a monastery of men and women and hosted a great synod
791.howItsDone: Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox Christians remember Saint Hilda of Whitby, and schools, colleges and churches in England and beyond bear her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine, and Gregory's letter about the old temples. Your line was bless, don't destroy.

In a house in the north of England, people keep arriving with questions for one woman. Ordinary people come, Bede says. So do kings and princes. They want to know what she thinks. She isn't a bishop or a queen. She's an abbess, and the people in her care have their own name for her.

Her name was Hilda, and she led the monastery at Whitby. It was a community of both men and women, under one abbess. Bede writes about her with real warmth. Her wisdom was so well known, he says, that rulers sought her counsel. She taught the people in her care to study the scriptures and to do what's right. She modeled the house on the earliest church in the Book of Acts, where no one was rich and no one was poor, because everything was shared. And everyone who knew her called her mother. Whitby is also where a great meeting happened, the synod of Whitby. The churches in the north had a problem. Some kept the customs they'd learned from the Irish monks of Iona, Columba's island. Others kept the customs of Rome. They didn't even agree on the date of Easter, so in one royal household, Bede says, one person could still be fasting while another was already celebrating. The king called both sides together at Hilda's house. Each side made its case. Hilda and her community held with the Irish custom. The king listened, and chose the Roman one, saying he would side with Peter, who holds the keys of heaven. Some who had argued for the Irish way went home to Iona. Bede doesn't record a word Hilda said that day. Her side lost, and she stayed, and went on leading her house.

Think of a woman whose judgment you trust: a grandmother, a teacher, a friend, someone at work. Notice what makes her wise, how she listens, what she's lived through, how little she rushes, and shape one real question you've been carrying into a single sentence, the kind you'd only ask someone like her. If you pray, give thanks for her; if not, just keep her face in mind.

Hilda. The abbess of Whitby kings came to for counsel, whose house hosted the great argument, and whom everyone called mother. That ends a week of Brigid, Benedict, Scholastica, Columba, Gregory and Augustine.
Your line: wisdom at whitby. Kings asked her; her people called her mother. See you tomorrow.
